questions.q: Write the complete ground-state electronic configuration of chlorine (Z=17) using the s,p,d,f notation and identify its period, group, and block in the modern periodic table.
questions.a: Chlorine (Z=17): 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁵ or [Ne]3s²3p⁵. Period = 3 (highest n=3), Group = 17 (7 valence electrons: 3s²3p⁵), Block = p-block (last electron enters p-orbital). A wrong answer like 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁴3d¹ reveals confusion about the Aufbau order (3d fills after 4s, not after 3p) and misunderstanding that period corresponds to the highest n, not the filling order.

questions.q: Explain why the 4th period contains 18 elements while the 3rd period contains only 8, even though both start with an s-orbital filling (4s and 3s respectively). Use the (n+l) rule in your explanation.
questions.a: In Period 3 (n=3), available subshells are 3s (n+l=3), 3p (n+l=4), and 3d (n+l=5). After 3s and 3p fill (8 electrons), the next available is 4s (n+l=4) which belongs to Period 4. Thus 3d (n+l=5) fills only after 4s. In Period 4, the filling sequence is 4s (n+l=4), then 3d (n+l=5), then 4p (n+l=5). Total orbitals = 1 (4s) + 5 (3d) + 3 (4p) = 9 orbitals → 18 electrons → 18 elements. A student who says "Period 4 has d-orbitals but Period 3 doesn't" misses the quantum mechanical reason — 3d exists but fills later due to higher (n+l) value.

questions.q: An element has the outer electronic configuration (n-1)d⁵ns¹. If n=4, identify the element, write its full configuration, and explain why this configuration is an exception to the Aufbau principle.
questions.a: For n=4: (n-1)d⁵ns¹ = 3d⁵4s¹. This is Chromium (Z=24). Full configuration: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁵4s¹ or [Ar]3d⁵4s¹. Expected by Aufbau: [Ar]3d⁴4s². The exception occurs because half-filled d-subshell (d⁵) and half-filled s-orbital (s¹) provide extra stability due to symmetrical electron distribution and exchange energy. A wrong answer giving [Ar]3d⁴4s² shows rigid application of Aufbau without considering stability of half-filled subshells. A student writing 4s¹3d⁵ instead of 3d⁵4s¹ reveals confusion about writing order (by n) vs filling order.

questions.q: Compare the electronic configurations of the Group 1 elements (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr). What pattern do you observe in their valence shell configuration? How does this pattern explain their similar chemical properties despite increasing atomic size?
questions.a: All Group 1 elements have valence configuration ns¹ (Li: 2s¹, Na: 3s¹, K: 4s¹, Rb: 5s¹, Cs: 6s¹, Fr: 7s¹). The pattern is constant: one electron in an s-orbital of the outermost shell. Similar properties arise because chemical behaviour is governed by valence electrons — all readily lose this single ns¹ electron to form M⁺ ions with noble gas configuration. Increasing size down the group lowers ionization energy (easier to lose electron), increasing reactivity, but the fundamental reaction type (loss of one electron) remains identical. A student citing "same number of valence electrons" without specifying ns¹ misses the orbital-specific nature — Group 2 also has "2 valence electrons" but they are ns², giving different chemistry.

questions.q: A student writes the electronic configuration of Copper (Z=29) as [Ar] 3d⁹4s². Evaluate this configuration. Is it correct? If not, provide the correct configuration and justify why the actual configuration differs from the Aufbau prediction.
questions.a: The student's configuration [Ar]3d⁹4s² is incorrect. Correct: [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹. Aufbau predicts 3d⁹4s², but the actual ground state has a fully-filled 3d¹⁰ subshell and half-filled 4s¹. This occurs because a completely filled d-subshell (d¹⁰) provides extra stability from maximum exchange energy and symmetrical charge distribution. The energy gap between 3d and 4s is small, so one electron from 4s promotes to 3d to achieve d¹⁰s¹. A student who says "Aufbau is always followed" doesn't understand that Aufbau is a guideline for building up, not a strict rule for ground states — stability of half/fully-filled subshells overrides it for Cr, Cu, Mo, Ag, Au, etc.

questions.q: Design a step-by-step method to determine the period, group, and block of any element given only its atomic number (Z), without memorizing the periodic table. Test your method on Z=114 and Z=117.
questions.a: Method: (1) Write electronic configuration using Aufbau/(n+l) rule. (2) Period = highest n in configuration. (3) Block = orbital type (s/p/d/f) of last added electron. (4) Group: For s-block = valence e⁻ count (1 or 2); p-block = 10 + valence e⁻ count; d-block = (n-1)d e⁻ + ns e⁻; f-block = separate (lanthanoids/actinoids). For Z=114: [Rn]5f¹⁴6d¹⁰7s²7p² → Period 7, p-block, Group 14 (10+4). For Z=117: [Rn]5f¹⁴6d¹⁰7s²7p⁵ → Period 7, p-block, Group 17 (10+7). A poor answer that just says "look at the table" fails to demonstrate the algorithmic connection between quantum numbers and table position. A good answer shows the configuration writing steps explicitly.
